pages.text: On the third of June, the whole school gathered in the hall. A banner read National Flood Disaster Day. Mr Adotey stood before them. “Today we remember a night in 2015 when a flood and a fire in Accra took the lives of many people,” he said. “We will speak plainly and with respect. Each number we say was a person.”

A banner read National Flood Disaster Day.
Mr Adotey stood before them.
“Today we remember a night in 2015 when a flood and a fire in Accra took the lives of many people,” he said.
“We will speak plainly and with respect.
Each number we say was a person.”
pages.alt: A school hall with pupils seated quietly beneath a banner and a single candle at the front.

pages.text: “On 3 June 2015, very heavy rain fell on Accra,” said Mr Adotey. “Floodwater rose around Kwame Nkrumah Circle. Many people took shelter at a filling station. The water carried fuel, and the station caught fire. Some people died in the flood, and many more died in the fire.”
sentences: “On 3 June 2015, very heavy rain fell on Accra,” said Mr Adotey.
“Floodwater rose around Kwame Nkrumah Circle.
Many people took shelter at a filling station.
The water carried fuel, and the station caught fire.
Some people died in the flood, and many more died in the fire.”
pages.alt: Dark clouds above a flooded junction with a distant glow, drawn without showing any people in harm.

pages.text: “How many died?” asked Efo. “Records differ,” said Mr Adotey. “Many reports say about 150, and some estimates go beyond 250. Reports also differ on how many died in the flood and how many in the fire. When numbers disagree, we do not choose the one we like. We say that it was a very large loss, and that we do not know the exact figure.”

“Records differ,” said Mr Adotey.
“Many reports say about 150, and some estimates go beyond 250.
Reports also differ on how many died in the flood and how many in the fire.
When numbers disagree, we do not choose the one we like.
We say that it was a very large loss, and that we do not know the exact figure.”
pages.alt: A notebook page with the numbers 150 and 250 and a question mark between them.

pages.text: “Why did it happen?” asked Bernice. “No single cause,” said Mr Adotey. “The rain was very heavy. Drains were blocked with silt and rubbish. Waterways had been built over. Many drains were made for a much smaller city and for lighter rain. Rules to protect waterways were not always enforced. A disaster usually has many causes joined together.”
sentences: “Why did it happen?” asked Bernice.
“No single cause,” said Mr Adotey.
“The rain was very heavy.
Drains were blocked with silt and rubbish.
Waterways had been built over.
Many drains were made for a much smaller city and for lighter rain.
Rules to protect waterways were not always enforced.
A disaster usually has many causes joined together.”
pages.alt: A diagram with arrows from rain, blocked drains, buildings on waterways and weak plans to a flooded street.

pages.text: “It did not end in 2015,” said Mr Adotey. “In May 2025, three hours of rain brought 132 millimetres, and reports say four or five people died and more than three thousand were forced from their homes. Accounts differ on the exact number. In early June 2026, rain flooded Kaneshie, Odawna, Adabraka and the Circle again.” The hall grew very quiet.

Accounts differ on the exact number.
In early June 2026, rain flooded Kaneshie, Odawna, Adabraka and the Circle again.” The hall grew very quiet.
pages.alt: A timeline with 2015, 2025 and 2026 and small rain clouds above each date.

pages.text: “What do we do with this?” asked Efo. Mr Adotey answered slowly. “First, we do not throw waste into drains. That is our part. Second, we ask leaders to keep drains clear, to protect waterways and wetlands, and to explain what they are doing. That is their part. And third, we stay safe: never shelter near fuel, never walk through floodwater, and keep away from open drains.”

Second, we ask leaders to keep drains clear, to protect waterways and wetlands, and to explain what they are doing.
That is their part.
And third, we stay safe: never shelter near fuel, never walk through floodwater, and keep away from open drains.”
pages.alt: Pupils write three headings on a board: Our part, Their part, Staying safe.

pages.text: Bernice wrote on her card: “I will tell my family to use the bin. I will write to my Assembly Member and ask what is being done about our drains.” Efo wrote: “I will count the blocked drains on our road and show the numbers.” Mr Adotey read the cards and nodded. “Remembering is not the end,” he said. “It is a beginning.”

pages.alt: Pupils write promise cards at their desks while the teacher reads one aloud.

pages.text: At noon, the pupils stood for a minute of silence. Outside, a light rain began to fall. It was gentle, and it ran away down the clean school gutter. Bernice looked at the water and then at Efo. “That is how it should always be,” she said. “Rain that goes where it belongs.” The end.

pages.alt: Pupils stand in the school yard in gentle rain beside a clear gutter, with heads bowed.

activities.question: What does Mr Adotey say to do when the numbers disagree?
options: Say the figures differ and that we do not know the exact one

activities.prompt: Mr Adotey says disasters have many causes. What might these be?
options: Heavy rain, blocked drains and building on waterways

activities.question: What are the three parts of Mr Adotey’s answer?
options: Our part, their part, staying safe
